clue.text: Carol eats pie, showing surprise

indicators.note: whatever eats something takes it inside itself, so one word swallows another

parts.note: to carol is to sing
a tart is a kind of pie

explanation.surface: A carol singer pauses mid-song to eat a pie, to everyone's amazement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'showing surprise' is the jump of a startled person, not delight; 'eats' means one word takes the other inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To start is to jump or flinch in shock, so someone starting is visibly reacting to a surprise.

clue.text: Entirely high in play

indicators.note: one word sits in another, placed within its letters

parts.note: to play with something is to toy with it
high and tall are synonyms

explanation.surface: Someone completely high during a theatre performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Totally and entirely are adverbs both meaning completely, wholly, without exception.

clue.text: Details oddly missing in marine kingdom

indicators.note: the kept letters are placed within another abbreviation

parts.note: RM stands for Royal Marine; its first letter opens the wrap

indicators.note: dropping the odd-numbered letters keeps only the even-placed ones

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word
the closing letter of the RM abbreviation

explanation.surface: An underwater realm described with gaps in the detail.
explanation.walkthrough: RM, a Royal Marine, goes round EAL, the even letters of 'Details'.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm is a kingdom, the domain ruled by a monarch.

clue.text: Unreliable clergyman supports setter asking permission to do a headstand

indicators.note: in a down entry the supporting word sits underneath, so it comes second
in a down clue standing on its head turns the phrase upside down, so it reads backwards

parts.note: the setter asking permission says 'Can I?'
a curate is an assistant member of the clergy

explanation.surface: A dubious vicar props up a crossword setter who wants to do a headstand.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter refers to themself as 'I', so asking permission is the question 'Can I?'; in a down entry 'supports' puts the clergyman underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inaccurate contains errors and so cannot be relied upon.

clue.text: Cutting crew smothering quiet one

indicators.note: to smother is to cover over completely, so one word wraps the others

parts.note: a gang is a crew of workers
the call for quiet
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A rowing crew muffling its one quiet member in a cutting remark.
explanation.definitionFit: Gashing means slashing a deep wound, a sense of cutting.

clue.text: Bodies quarrel in vacuous sessions

indicators.note: one word goes within the remaining outer letters
vacuous means empty, so the word is emptied of its inside, leaving only its ends

parts.note: the first and last letters
a tiff is a small quarrel

explanation.surface: Delegates bicker during pointless meetings.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiffs is slang for corpses, dead bodies.

clue.text: Identical Welsh politician in the Home Counties

indicators.note: the politician is placed within the region's abbreviation

parts.note: the Home Counties around London are in the South East of England
AM was Assembly Member, a member of the Welsh Assembly

explanation.surface: A Welsh politician who looks just the same living in the commuter belt.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties surrounding London.
explanation.definitionFit: Same and identical are adjectives both meaning exactly alike.

clue.text: Somewhat wearisome trick-or-treaters of similar dimensions

indicators.note: somewhat means only partly, so just part of the following words is used

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Children going door to door at Halloween are a bit tiresome.
explanation.definitionFit: Isometric means having equal measurements, from Greek for equal measure.

clue.text: Surprising her with gift that's carried by rail and road

definitions.text: that's carried by rail and road

indicators.note: something surprising is unexpected, hinting that these letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Surprising someone with a present delivered by train and lorry.
explanation.definitionFit: Freight is goods transported in bulk by trains, lorries, ships or planes.

clue.text: City's old power unit going into reverse has radioactive core

parts.note: a standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: going into reverse means travelling backwards, so the unit is read back to front

parts.note: the watt is the unit of power

indicators.note: a core is the very centre, so only the middle letter is taken

parts.note: the sixth of eleven letters

explanation.surface: A city's ageing power plant goes into decline and has a radioactive reactor core.
explanation.definitionFit: Ottawa is the capital city of Canada.

clue.text: Mum's worried about emergency doctor initially being sent for

indicators.note: worried describes agitation, so the letters are churned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, dropping the apostrophe
on can mean about, as in a talk on a subject

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of each of the words before it

parts.note: the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A worried mother talks about the emergency doctor who is being called out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being sent for' is the definition; 'Summoned' works there because both are past participles.
explanation.definitionFit: To be summoned is to be called or sent for to come somewhere.

clue.text: Cold inside — to do with the weather reaching a culmination

indicators.note: the abbreviation goes inside the longer word

parts.note: climatic means relating to climate
C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Cold weather indoors builds to a peak.
explanation.walkthrough: C slips into CLIMATIC after its A.
explanation.definitionFit: A climax is the culmination of events, so climactic describes reaching that high point.

clue.text: Man would shortly get trimmed at barrier

indicators.note: trimming clips the end off, so the last letter is cut away

parts.note: 'he would' shortened is he'd
taken as written before being cut

explanation.surface: A man will soon have a haircut at the fence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trimmed' fits the surface of a hedge, which is exactly what makes it misleading.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedge is a row of bushes forming a barrier or boundary.

clue.text: Earthy language used by Independent puzzler working around western county

indicators.note: around means encircling, so the setter's name surrounds the county

parts.note: Anax is a setter for the Independent; this is its opening part
Glos is short for Gloucestershire, a county in western England
the rest of the setter's pseudonym Anax
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A fellow crossword setter swears like a trooper in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: ANAX wraps GLOS, then ON follows. Anglo-Saxon is the plain blunt vocabulary of English, especially swear words.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglo-Saxon words are the blunt, often crude core of English, so earthy language is a fair idiom for them.

clue.text: Some jittery people back centrepiece of funerary rite

indicators.note: going back means reading the run of letters from right to left
some means only a portion, so the letters lie within the following words

parts.note: the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Nervous mourners hang back from the main event of a funeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A pyre is the heap of wood on which a body is burnt, central to a cremation.

clue.text: Sound of bells cut short by pulse

indicators.note: cutting something short removes its final letter

parts.note: a peal is a ringing of bells

explanation.surface: Church bells interrupted by a heartbeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulse' suggests a heartbeat but here means an edible seed of a legume.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are edible legume seeds such as lentils, beans and peas.

clue.text: Nurse inclined to be joining up

parts.note: EN is an Enrolled Nurse
a ship that is listing leans to one side

explanation.surface: A nurse feels inclined to sign up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inclined' reads as willing but means tilting, as a ship does.
explanation.definitionFit: Enlisting means enrolling in the armed forces, signing on or joining up.

clue.text: Stir green tea without hesitation to promote new growth

indicators.note: stirring mixes things around, so the letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
er is a sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: Brewing green tea without a pause is supposed to rejuvenate you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but means 'with outside', so ER joins the mix rather than leaving it.
explanation.definitionFit: To regenerate is to grow again or renew tissue, so encouraging fresh growth.

clue.text: Time exhibition's beginning, with support of artist

indicators.note: a word's beginning is its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter
RA is a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: An exhibition opens on time thanks to an artist's backing.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the supporting piece sits below, so RA follows E.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a period of time, an age in history.

clue.text: Being logical, I call at any trouble

indicators.note: trouble suggests disorder, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A methodical person announces they will visit whenever there's a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: An analytical mind reasons step by step, which is to say logically.

clue.text: Feed new leader around teatime when chief finally leaves

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so the opening letter

parts.note: the first letter

indicators.note: the letter that leaves is removed from the phrase

parts.note: around four o'clock, the traditional British teatime, is four-ish

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word before it

parts.note: the last letter, the one taken away

explanation.surface: A new boss serving food at teatime, then leaving once the chief goes.
explanation.walkthrough: Four o'clock is classic British afternoon-tea time; drop its F and put N in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To nourish is to provide food needed for growth and health, to feed.

clue.text: Raise false alarm about railway going over rising water current

indicators.note: in a down entry one part lying over another comes first

parts.note: c for circa, about
an abbreviation for railway

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means going upwards, so the word reads bottom to top

parts.note: a flow is a current of water

explanation.surface: Someone panics needlessly about a railway bridge over a rising stream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising water' suggests a flood, but 'rising' acts on 'water current' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To cry wolf, from Aesop's fable, is to raise false alarms until nobody believes you.

clue.text: Company lawyer's finale

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company
DA is a District Attorney, an American prosecutor

explanation.surface: A corporate lawyer's last act.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as 'has' or 'is' joining the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A coda is the concluding passage of a piece of music, its finale.

clue.text: Woman got up when queen forgot her lines

indicators.note: in a down entry getting up means rising, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: ER is Elizabeth Regina
an actor who dries forgets their lines

explanation.surface: An actress playing a queen stood up and blanked on her lines.
explanation.walkthrough: To dry is theatre slang for forgetting one's lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Deirdre is a woman's first name, from the Irish legend of Deirdre of the Sorrows.

clue.text: Visitor's sudden blow gathering energy

indicators.note: to gather something is to draw it in, so one word holds the other

parts.note: a gust is a sudden blast of wind
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A caller is hit by a sudden powerful punch.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A guest is someone invited to visit a home or event.

clue.text: Note agreement to practise for unpleasant condition

parts.note: E is a musical note
yes expresses agreement
to train is to practise

explanation.surface: A memo about an agreed training plan for a disagreeable ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyestrain is a tired, aching condition of the eyes from overuse, an unpleasant ailment.

clue.text: Nurse baffled by old characters

indicators.note: someone baffled is confused, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nurse is puzzled by some elderly patients.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old characters' reads as eccentric elderly people but means ancient letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Runes are letters of ancient Germanic alphabets, old written characters.

clue.text: Touring rugby player picks up new lubricant

indicators.note: in a down entry picking something up raises it, so the letters read upwards

parts.note: N for new
oil is a lubricant

explanation.surface: A visiting rugby star buys a fresh tube of liniment.
explanation.walkthrough: The British and Irish Lions are a rugby union team drawn from four nations that tours abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A player chosen for the British and Irish Lions touring side is called a Lion.

clue.text: Islander one to go mad about current number

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the verb wraps round the numeral

parts.note: to flip is to lose one's temper
Roman numeral one
I is the symbol for electric current
No. is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: An islander goes crazy over the latest number.
explanation.definitionFit: A Filipino is a native of the Philippines, an archipelago of islands.

clue.text: Be leaving bandeaux around old Chinese summer capital

indicators.note: around here means moved about, so the remaining letters are rearranged
the letters that leave are removed from the word

parts.note: taken as written
the letters B and E are removed

explanation.surface: Discarding headbands around the old imperial summer retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: A bandeau is a narrow headband. Remove one B and one E, then rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Xanadu, or Shangdu, was Kublai Khan's summer capital, famed through Coleridge's poem.

clue.text: Paper-wrapped pig for dictator

parts.note: The Sun is a British newspaper
a hog is a pig

explanation.surface: A pig wrapped in newspaper is presented as a tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: A shogun was a hereditary military ruler of Japan, effectively a dictator.

clue.text: Complete flipper I get rid of

parts.note: a fin is a flipper
taken as written
to shed is to discard
